newsitem.title: UK: Statements by G7 leaders in Berlin on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Statements by G7 leaders in Berlin on EMU.

text.p: Though Europe's economic and monetary union took a back seat to foreign exchange markets as the focus of the Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Berlin on Satruday, following are the few key comments made in Berlin from G7 officials about EMU:

UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said the G7 "did not have a substantial discussion on EMU" but that German Finance Minister Theo Waigel gave a report summarising the Dublin summit of European leaders last year.

Asked whether there was any U.S. concern about the potential impact the introduction of the euro could have, Clarke said "it seems to me, the three non-Europeans felt no need to initiate a discussion (on the euro."
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told a news conference "we spent very little time discussing EMU...Almost no discussion at all."

When Clarke was asked if the U.S. was concerned about the impact of the Maastricht criteria on European growth levels, Clarke said "the key thing is for all of us is to get unemployment to the lowest sustainable levels."

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said Germany's record jobless level of 4.66 million hit in January should not keep Germany from meeting Maatsricht criteria for membership in the planned single European currency in January 1999.

Regarding Germany's efforts to get its finances in order to meet EMU criteria, Tietmeyer said "they will try to hold it (the deficit) below (the three-percent goal stated in the Maastricht Treaty). It is not an easy task, but I hope they will succeed."

He also said he did not understand the irritation regarding Italy's bid to enter the currency union and noted that there has been no discussion among central bankers to give preference to or discriminate against certain countries. He said G7 leaders did not discuss in Berlin entry of certain countries into EMU.
Last week, a Financial Times newspaper article suggested European Union monetary officials were planning to delay Italy's entry into EMU.
But Tietmeyer said at the G7 meeting that Italy must be treated equally in its bid to enter EMU.
Italian Treasury and Budget Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Saturday he did not see Italy meeting an original forecast for 2.0-percent 1997 growth.

"Italy willnot meet its original two-percent growth goal for GDP in 1997," he said. "The trend has been positive in the last months, but the 1997 average growth will be above one percent and at most, 1.5 percent."
Ciampi added that Italy's public sector deficit to gross domestic product ratio would stand at 6.8 percent in 1996, according to new accounting methods approved by the Eurostat statistics office.

French finance minister Jean Arthuis declined to comment on reported tensions between Germany, which many believe would like EMU membership to be initially resticted to a hard core of northern European countries, and Italy, which with Spain and Portugal, wants to help launch the euro in January 1999.

Arthuis said a decision would be made in early 1998 on which countries would be eligible for the 1999 start and that he hoped any country not taking part in EMU at its proposed start date in 1999 will be able to join as soon as possible.
"We must hope that anyone who is not in the first group can join as quickly as possible," Arthuis said.
Waigel also said it was too early to speculate which countries would not be able to meet Maastricht criteria and launch the euro in January 1999.

"It is just the start of February. Every country has a chance to meet the criteria. Only at the start of next year, when the figures are produced, will we be able to say" who will be able to join, Waigel said.
In response to fears the euro would not be stable, Waigel said "that fear is unjustified. The euro will be just as stable as the mark."
